analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers put their phone numbers on a national list blocking most telemarketing calls.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the do-not-call bill 412-8 in the House and 95-0 in the Senate within a day, and the president signed it into law four days after it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This law gives the Federal Trade Commission explicit legal authority to run the national do-not-call registry, the free list where households can register their phone numbers so most telemarketers may not call them. Congress moved to enact it after a federal judge ruled the FTC lacked the power to enforce the registry, which threatened to shut it down. It passed both chambers with almost no opposition and became Public Law 108-82.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households: anyone who registers a phone number on the list can stop most commercial sales calls. The law also protects consumers' existing expectations, since the registry had been accepting sign-ups since early 2003 and the court ruling put it at risk.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that the FTC is authorized under the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act to implement and enforce a national do-not-call registry.
Ratifies the do-not-call registry provision of the Telemarketing Sales Rule that the FTC put in effect on March 31, 2003, preserving the list consumers had already joined.
Passed the House 412-8 and the Senate 95-0, and was signed by the president on September 29, 2003, becoming Public Law 108-82.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing firms and outbound call centers, which lose the ability to call numbers on the registry and bear the cost of scrubbing their call lists. Charities, political campaigns, surveys, and companies a consumer already does business with are not covered by the registry.

drawbacks.text: The registry does not stop every unwanted call: political campaigns, charities, surveys, and companies the consumer has an existing business relationship with remain free to call, limits written into the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule that this law ratifies rather than tightens.
The bill is a one-sentence ratification of the FTC's existing rule; it adds no new enforcement resources or tougher penalties beyond what the FTC already had under the Telemarketing Act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary households is large and immediate — millions signed up for the registry, and the law protected it from being struck down. The cost falls on a specific industry, telemarketers, which warned of lost sales and jobs. The main honest criticism is scope, not design: the law leaves political, charitable, and business-relationship calls untouched, so it reduces but does not eliminate unwanted calls.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 412-8 and the Senate passed it without amendment 95-0 on the same day, and the president signed it four days after introduction, making it Public Law 108-82.

narrative.text: The FTC's do-not-call registry took effect March 31, 2003, and Congress acted to ratify it and confirm the FTC's authority to run it.
The House passed the bill 412-8 (Roll no. 521) and the Senate passed it without amendment 95-0 (Record Vote 365), both on September 25, 2003.
The president signed it on September 29, 2003, and it became Public Law 108-82.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers who signed up for the registry are better off: the law protected the list from being struck down. Telemarketing firms, which had challenged the FTC's authority, lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who signed up for the list

for.name: W. J. (Billy) Tauzin
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and had his committee discharged so the House could take it up and pass it within a day of introduction.

for.name: 95 of 99 Senate members
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill without amendment, 95-0, on the same day the House passed it.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on September 29, 2003.

against.name: Telemarketing industry
against.role: Direct marketers and outbound call centers
against.what_they_did: Opposed the registry and supported the court challenge to the FTC's authority that this bill was passed to override.

against.name: US District Court (Oklahoma)
against.what_they_did: Ruled the FTC lacked statutory authority to enforce the do-not-call registry, prompting Congress to move this ratification bill within days.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous across both parties: 192 of 205 House Democrats and 219 of 228 House Republicans voted yes, and the Senate passed it 95-0 with no no votes from either party.

industries.note: The registry bars commercial telemarketers from calling numbers on the list, cutting off their core sales channel for households that opt out. Consumers gain peace and quiet exactly where the industry loses access. The industry fought the FTC's rule in court before Congress ratified it.

These callers are not covered by the do-not-call registry, so they can keep calling while their commercial competitors are blocked. Their relative access to households improves even though the law imposes no rules on them.
